options: The percentage decline from the highest value a portfolio has reached so far down to its current value
The total return of a portfolio over its entire history
The standard deviation of daily returns
The number of losing trades in a row
questions.explain: Drawdown measures peak-to-current decline, capturing the real experience of loss from a prior high point, not just overall volatility or return.

questions.q: In the worked example, the portfolio ended up profitable (1135.94 vs. a starting 1000) but still had a -22.23% max drawdown. What does this demonstrate?
options: A portfolio can be profitable overall while still having lived through a severe peak-to-trough decline along the way
The simulation must contain a bug, since a profitable portfolio cannot have a large drawdown
Drawdown is only meaningful for portfolios that lose money overall
Positive drift always prevents meaningful drawdowns
questions.explain: Ending profitable says nothing about the ride along the way -- a 22% decline from a peak, with no guarantee of recovery at the time, is a real experience even in a strategy that eventually recovers and gains.

questions.q: Why can two portfolios with identical volatility have very different maximum drawdowns?
options: Drawdown depends on the SEQUENCE and clustering of gains/losses over time, which volatility (having no memory of order) does not capture
Volatility and drawdown are always mathematically identical
Drawdown only applies to portfolios with negative expected returns
Maximum drawdown is randomly assigned and unrelated to actual returns
questions.explain: Volatility treats an up day and down day of equal size as identical regardless of order; drawdown is explicitly about how losses cluster in time, so identical volatility can produce very different drawdown experiences.

questions.q: In a drawdown-limit structure with soft, hard, and kill-switch thresholds, what distinguishes a hard limit from a soft limit?
options: A hard limit triggers automatic de-risking with no discretion involved, while a soft limit only triggers a review
A soft limit always shuts down the strategy entirely
A hard limit and soft limit are the same thing, just at different drawdown percentages with identical actions
A hard limit only applies to portfolios with positive expected returns
questions.explain: A soft limit prompts reassessment with no automatic action; a hard limit forces a pre-specified de-risking or exit mechanically, with no in-the-moment discretion.

questions.q: Why are real drawdown limits decided in advance (while calm) rather than improvised when a drawdown is actually happening?
options: Being deep in a drawdown is the worst possible time to trust your own in-the-moment judgment about whether the losses will reverse
Drawdown limits decided in advance are always less effective than real-time decisions
Regulations require all risk limits to be set a fixed number of years in advance
There is no real reason -- the timing of the decision doesn't matter
questions.explain: The same discipline as Lesson 19's leaky-strategy lesson: a rule locked in ahead of time and enforced mechanically protects a portfolio precisely when emotional, in-the-moment judgment is least trustworthy.
